title: Collaborative Document Editor (Google Docs)
summary: Design a real-time collaborative editor where many users edit the same document simultaneously.
statement: Design a Google Docs-style editor. Multiple users edit one document at once, see each other cursors and changes within a fraction of a second, and the document converges to the same state for everyone, with history and offline edits. Start by clarifying requirements and estimating scale, then design the system and defend your decisions.
initialGuidance: Clarify the users, the main journeys, and what is explicitly out of scope before drawing anything.
Estimate read and write volume and storage growth; the numbers decide which components you need.
Name the guarantees you will offer (consistency, durability, availability) and the trade-offs behind them.
Write down assumptions as you make them and revisit them when requirements change.
coreFunctionalRequirements: Multiple users edit the same document.

requirementQuestions.question: How many documents, and how many simultaneous editors per document?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Sets read and write rates and storage growth, which decide whether a single node can cope.

requirementQuestions.question: How quickly must remote edits appear?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Defines which paths need caching, precomputation, or regional placement.

requirementQuestions.question: What convergence guarantee is needed for concurrent edits?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Selects between strong and eventual models and shapes conflict handling.

requirementQuestions.question: Rich text, comments, and permissions?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Fixes what is in and out of the design so effort goes to what matters.

requirementQuestions.question: Should editing continue offline?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines redundancy and failover design, and which features may degrade instead of failing.

requirementQuestions.question: How is history retained and how large can documents be?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines the data model, retention, and storage choices.

workloadAssumptions.illustrativeNote: All numbers below are illustrative examples for practice and are not benchmarks. Real answers depend on the requirements the candidate negotiates.

estimationPrompts: How many operation messages per second across the platform?
How large is the operation log per document?
How many connections must each server hold?

keyDecisions.question: How are concurrent edits merged?
considerations: Operational Transformation with a central server ordering operations.
CRDTs allow merging without central ordering at metadata cost.
Both converge but differ in complexity and overhead.

keyDecisions.question: How are collaborators connected?
considerations: All editors of a document connect to the same server instance or shard.
Route by document ID with consistent hashing.
Failover and reconnection with state catch-up.

keyDecisions.question: How is the document stored?
considerations: Append operation log and periodic snapshots.
Rebuild state from the latest snapshot plus recent operations.

keyDecisions.question: How are cursors shared?
considerations: Lightweight ephemeral messages not stored durably.

keyDecisions.question: How is offline editing merged?
considerations: Queue local operations and rebase on reconnect.

tradeoffs.tension: Central server simplicity versus decentralised flexibility and memory overhead.
Faster loads versus storage and compute.
Simple ordering versus hot document limits.

commonMistakes: Locking the document or paragraphs for one editor.
Persisting every keystroke as a separate database write.
No plan for server failure mid-session.
followUps: How do you support comments and suggestions?
How do you scale a document with 10,000 viewers?
How do you do undo in a collaborative setting?
How do you migrate a document between servers?
